# Abstract

In this project I check whether the EUR/PLN exchange rate is linked to the gap
between Polish and euro-area interest rates. I use monthly data from
`r format(min(df$date), "%Y")` to `r format(max(df$date), "%Y")`
(`r nrow(df)` months). I first test if the series are stationary, then I look for
a long-run link using cointegration tests and an ARDL model. I also add Brent oil
as a control and use a simple ARIMA model as a benchmark. [Write the main result
here once the models are run — for example, whether I find a long-run link and
how fast the exchange rate goes back to it.]

# Introduction

The link between exchange rates and interest rates is a classic topic in
international finance. The main idea is uncovered interest parity (UIP): if one
country has higher interest rates, its currency is expected to weaken by about
the same amount, so investors do not get a free profit. In practice this idea
often fails in the short run but works better over longer periods
[@chinn2004; @fama1984].

Poland is a good case to study. It has its own currency, floats freely, and sits
next to the euro area. The National Bank of Poland (NBP) often keeps interest
rates quite different from the European Central Bank (ECB). This gap got very big
in 2022–2023, when the NBP raised rates much higher than the ECB, and then both
banks started cutting. This gives me a lot of useful variation to work with.

My main question is simple: **is there a stable long-run link between the EUR/PLN
rate and the NBP–ECB interest rate gap, and if the rate moves away from that
link, how fast does it come back?**

# Literature Review

**Exchange rates and UIP.** A famous result by @meese1983 showed that complex
exchange-rate models often cannot beat a simple random walk in short-run
forecasts. That is why I also include a basic ARIMA model as a benchmark.
@fama1984 found that interest rate gaps are biased predictors of future currency
moves (the "forward premium puzzle"). Later, @chinn2004 showed that UIP works
much better over long horizons, which is why I focus on a long-run model instead
of a short-run one.

**Interest rates and exchange rates in the long run.** @macdonald2000 found a
long-run link between real exchange rates and real interest rate gaps for the G7
countries. This supports the idea of treating the interest rate gap as a long-run
driver of the exchange rate.

**Emerging markets.** Things can look different for emerging markets.
@frankel2010 found that the forward bias is actually smaller for emerging-market
currencies than for big currencies. This is useful background when I read my
results for the zloty.

**Methods I rely on.** For the methods I follow the standard time-series toolkit:
unit-root tests [@dickey1979; @kwiatkowski1992], residual-based cointegration
tests [@engle1987; @phillips1990], the Johansen [-@johansen1988] system test, and
the ARDL bounds test by @pesaran2001. I lean on the ARDL test because it still
works when some variables are stationary and others are not — which is likely
here, since interest rate gaps are often close to the border between the two.

# Data

```{r data-summary}
desc <- df %>%
  summarise(`Obs.` = n(),
            Start = format(min(date), "%Y-%m"),
            End   = format(max(date), "%Y-%m"))
kable(desc, caption = "Sample coverage")
```

I use monthly data. The variables are:

- **EUR/PLN** — the NBP Table A exchange rate, taken at the end of each month.
- **NBP reference rate** — Poland's main policy rate, set to the value in force at
  month-end.
- **ECB main refinancing rate (MRR)** — the euro-area policy rate.
- **Interest rate gap** — NBP rate minus ECB rate, in percentage points.
- **Brent oil (control)** — monthly oil price in USD (in logs). Poland imports
  oil, so the oil price can affect the zloty through trade.

```{r desc-stats}
vars_tbl <- df %>%
  select(eurpln, rate_diff, any_of(c("nbp_rate","ecb_rate","brent"))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "v") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(Mean = mean(v), SD = sd(v), Min = min(v), Max = max(v), .groups = "drop")
kable(vars_tbl, digits = 2, caption = "Descriptive statistics")
```


# Methodology

I work in four steps.

**Step 1 — Check for unit roots.** First I test if each series is stationary.
I use two tests together: the ADF test [@dickey1979], where the null is a unit
root (non-stationary), and the KPSS test [@kwiatkowski1992], where the null is
stationary. Using both is safer. I call a series I(1) only if it looks
non-stationary in levels but stationary after taking first differences.

**Step 2 — Test for cointegration.** If the variables are I(1), I check if they
move together in the long run. I use the Phillips–Ouliaris test [@phillips1990],
which is the Engle–Granger [-@engle1987] idea with the right critical values, and
the Johansen [-@johansen1988] test, which finds how many long-run links exist.

**Step 3 — ARDL bounds test.** The interest rate gap might be stationary, not
I(1). To be safe I use the ARDL bounds test [@pesaran2001] as my main model. It
works with any mix of stationary and non-stationary variables. It gives me the
long-run effect and an error-correction model (ECM), which shows how fast the
rate returns to its long-run level after a shock. I pick the lag lengths with the
AIC.

**Step 4 — ARIMA benchmark.** I also fit a simple ARIMA model on the exchange
rate alone, keeping the last 12 months aside to test forecasts. This tells me if
the interest rate information actually helps, compared to a model that only uses
the past of the exchange rate [@meese1983].

I finish with checks on the model: tests for leftover correlation in the errors
(Breusch–Godfrey), changing variance (Breusch–Pagan), normal errors
(Jarque–Bera), and wrong functional form (Ramsey RESET). I also run a
Zivot–Andrews test that allows one break in the data, and a CUSUM test for
stability over time.

# Results

## Unit-root tests

```{r unit-root}
if (!is.null(res) && !is.null(res$unit_root_orders)) {
  ur <- tibble(Series = names(res$unit_root_orders),
               `Integration order` = as.character(res$unit_root_orders))
  kable(ur, caption = "Order of integration (from ADF + KPSS).")
} else cat("Run 02_analysis.R to fill this table.")
```

[Say which series are I(1). Most importantly, say if the interest rate gap is
stationary or not, because this decides whether normal cointegration is allowed
or whether only the ARDL bounds test is valid.]

## Cointegration

```{r coint}
if (!is.null(res) && !is.null(res$po_test)) {
  cat("Phillips–Ouliaris statistic:",
      round(as.numeric(res$po_test$statistic), 3),
      "| p-value:", format.pval(res$po_test$p.value), "\n")
} else cat("Run 02_analysis.R to fill this in.\n")
```

[Report the Johansen result from the console and say how many long-run links
there are. Compare it with the bounds test below.]

## ARDL bounds test and error correction

```{r ardl}
if (!is.null(res) && !is.null(res$bounds)) {
  cat("ARDL bounds F-statistic:",
      round(as.numeric(res$bounds$statistic), 3), "\n")
  cat("(Compare with the Pesaran et al. 2001 bounds for case 3.)\n")
} else cat("Run 02_analysis.R to fill this in.\n")
```

[Report the long-run effect of the interest rate gap and the speed-of-adjustment
(ECM) term. A negative and significant ECM term means the rate does return to its
long-run level; its size tells me how much of the gap closes each month.]
